result.rationale: The diff confirms the mechanism: in handleNewBooking, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` adds all collective hosts' calendars, but persistence only does `connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id }`, so only the first is stored. Deferred flows shown in the diff (confirm.handler.ts, webhook.ts/paypal-webhook.ts) rebuild the event as `booking.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : ...`, a single-element array, so hosts 2..N's calendars are lost and their calendar events never created. This is a verifiable correctness defect introduced by the change.

judged_text: Only evt.destinationCalendar[0] is connected to the Booking's single destinationCalendar relation, so the additional collective hosts' destination calendars pushed into the array are never persisted anywhere. Deferred-creation flows rebuild CalendarEvent from the persisted booking — confirm.handler.ts and the stripe/paypal payment-success webhooks wrap booking.destinationCalendar in a one-element array — so confirming or taking payment on a multi-host collective booking creates calendar events on only the first host's calendar and hosts 2..N never receive them.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar changed to an array and handleNewBooking.ts pushes additional collective hosts’ destination calendars into evt.destinationCalendar (teamDestinationCalendars). However, when persisting the booking it still connects only the first element: `connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id }` (handleNewBooking.ts). Later “deferred creation” paths rebuild CalendarEvent from the persisted Booking’s singular `booking.destinationCalendar` and wrap it into a one-element array (e.g., confirm.handler.ts, stripe/paypal webhook handlers), so those flows can only ever see one destination calendar and thus will create calendar events for host #1 only, not hosts 2..N.
